title: Shopping and paying
goal: Order, ask the price, and pay — while meeting for the first time the expression *mig langar*, which puts "I" not as the doer but as the target.
bekal: order food and drinks with *ég ætla að fá* and *mig langar í*
ask the price and pay by card
make adjectives agree when they describe an object

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Á kaffihúsinu
dialogs.intro: A small bakery in the town center. Búdí orders on his own for the first time and leaves with a culinary discovery.

lines.speaker: Afgreiðslukona:
lines.text: Góðan daginn! Get ég aðstoðað þig?
lines.id: Good afternoon! Can I help you?
lines.literal: good day-the! can I help you?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Já, takk. Mig langar í kaffi og einn snúð.
lines.id: Yes, thanks. I'd like a coffee and a snúður.
lines.literal: me(object) longs into coffee and one snúður.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: Large, thanks. How much is this?

lines.speaker: Afgreiðslukona:
lines.text: Að sjálfsögðu. Allir borga með korti hér.
lines.id: Of course. Everyone pays by card here.
lines.literal: of-course self-said. all pay with card here.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Gott, því ég á engan pening.
lines.id: Good, because I don't have any cash.
lines.literal: good, because I have no money.

lines.speaker: Afgreiðslukona:
lines.id: Nobody needs it. Would you like a receipt?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Nei, takk. Eitt enn: hvað heitir þetta brauð?
lines.id: No, thanks. One more thing: what is this bread called?
lines.literal: no, thanks. one more: what is-called this bread?

lines.speaker: Afgreiðslukona:
lines.text: Það er rúgbrauð. Það er bakað í jörðinni!
lines.id: That's rúgbrauð. It's baked in the ground!
lines.literal: it is rye-bread. it is baked in ground-the.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Í jörðinni? Þá verð ég að smakka það.
lines.id: In the ground? Then I have to try it.
lines.literal: in ground-the? then must I to taste it.

notes: **Mig langar í kaffi — and "I" in this sentence is not the doer.** The form is *mig*, not *ég*: literally "me longs into coffee". Icelandic has a whole set of expressions like this, and they all put the person as the target, not the doer. Unit 14 covers them fully; for now use this one as a ready-made phrase.

**Three ways to order, from most casual to most polite**: *Ég ætla að fá …* (I'll have …), *Mig langar í …* (I'd like …), *Gæti ég fengið …?* (could I get …?). All three are polite; the first is the one you'll hear most at the counter.

**Adjectives change too when they describe an object**: *stór* → *stóran*, *lítill* → *lítinn*. The endings **-an** and **-inn** mark þolfall karlkyn — the form you'll need most often, because so many things are kk.

**Engan pening — "no money at all".** *Enginn* (no, none) changes form like an adjective: *enginn* → *engan* as an object. Notice the sentence does **not** use *ekki*; *enginn* already carries its own negation.

**Iceland has almost completely given up cash.** Cards are accepted everywhere, including hot dog stands and public toilets. Carrying banknotes is often more trouble than it's worth — many places have no change.

**Rúgbrauð really is baked in the ground.** Rye dough is buried in hot sand near a hot spring for 24 hours. It's sweet and dense, served with butter and herring — one of the foods most worth trying in Iceland.

grammars.title: Vilja and mig langar
body: Two ways to say "want", and the difference isn't politeness but **grammar**: one uses *ég*, the other uses *mig*.
after: ⚠️ *Vil* means **want**, not "will". *Ég vil fara* = I want to go, not I will go. English speakers fall into this trap constantly — the words look alike, but the meaning can shift a lot.
The six forms of *vilja*: *ég vil, þú vilt, hann vill, við viljum, þið viljið, þeir vilja*. Note *vill* with double l for *hann* — the only form with a doubled letter.

grammars.title: Adjectives describing an object
body: After describing the subject (unit 3), adjectives now describe the object. Only the karlkyn form really changes; the other two barely move.
after: The markers to recognize: **-an** for kk, **-a** for kvk, and hk stays as the base form. If in doubt, listen to the ending — those two letters make the difference.

The *Góðan daginn!* you've been saying since unit 1 turns out to be adjective + noun in **þolfall**: literally "(may you have) a good day". The greeting you already know has been quietly teaching you the grammar.

blocks.title: Two foods you should know by name
items: **Skyr** isn't yogurt but a fat-free soft cheese, eaten like yogurt, and made by Icelanders since the settlement age. It's the national breakfast and in every supermarket.

**Pylsa** is the Icelandic hot dog, and the standard order is *ein með öllu* — "one with everything": sweet mustard, remoulade, fried onions, and raw onions. That's the only sentence you need at a hot dog stand.
